paragraphs: As the bells of St. Thomas Cathedral rang out, echoing across the awakening downtown area of the small Midwestern town nestled in the recesses carved by glaciers long gone into the rivers and the Gulf, it seemed like just another autumn Monday morning. The sun crept across the sky, its rays sweeping across the structures along the river, the tallest of those structures casting longer and longer shadows over areas to the west like fingers reaching out, hands attempting to cover and perhaps smother those areas like the industrial smoke pouring from the myriad factories and workshops beginning to groan into gear for the start of the week as more and more cars began to fill the streets, contributing to the polluted air while those between vehicle and structures in increasing numbers begin to fill the streets and populate the businesses and offices downtown, so accustomed to breathing in that pollution, that darkness, that they are no longer even aware of its existence, if the ever were at all. The bells toll for six and the town begins to stretch out like those shadows and by the time those neighborhoods beneath the shadows rise in full by the toll of seven, the overshadowed residential neighborhoods are ready to carry one with their normal routine on what will turn out to be the most abnormal day the residents have experienced to date, and it will prove to be the first of many to come.

Within those shadowy fingers, which do not seem to carress so much as attempt to posses, among dozens of similar buildings making up the neighborhood in the northeast sector of the town, there are four buildings in a row along a street one block over from the town's main thoroughfare that are own by a single local entity and together those residential buildings camaflouge what the locals refer to as "Juvie Jail" as those houses are populated with young people who lives have been disrupted either though their own actions or those of others and the state has moved them into the residence either for protection or punishment. The buildings are currently alive with activity as their structure routines has had the residents busy since the first toll of the six o'clock hour and at the final bell marking seven o'clock we see through the window of one of those buildings that one of the residents has seemingly finished all of her morning activities as she leans against the window sill, looking out toward the building casting its ugly pall over the city.

This is Jackie. She stands in the window, looking out, watching for nothing, expecting nothing. There is a depth to her stare, her amber-colored eyes reflecting on the perfectly polished window, her cinnamon hair drifting down her shoulders, her left hand twirling her hair subtly while she collects her thoughts, pulls herself back from the past and the pain and back to this moment. Her reflection-- literally and metaphirical-- will soon be coming to an end, she knows, which is why she always attempts to rise early and be done with all of her morning tasks because by the time those bells at St. Thomas strike the quarter-hour, quiet and calm will be a beloved memory when the other nine girls who share this residence and this floor begin to come to life in a cacophony of energy of which only teenage human females are capable, especially in large groups.

And now, even as her thoughts begin to drift back from her own life's mysteries to the mundane Monday minutiae, she hears the footsteps coming from the hall, slowly becomes aware of the music someone is playing down the hall, and braces herself as she hears the doorknob being turned.
She also turns. Toward the door and away from the reflections just as the door swings inward with a crash.
"...YOU MAKE ME FEEL! AND YOU MAKE ME FEEL LIKE A NATURAL WOMAN!"

Jackie blinked and looked at her roommate, Maggie, standing in the doorway, arms spread wide and into the air, dramatically. And she stayed there... and stayed there. Finally, as Jackie watched, she shifted her eyes down to Jackie, let what seemed to be every molecule of air in her body out in a dramatic exhale, and said, "Ugh. You are a _terrible_ background singer," and closed the door behind her.

"Sorry," Jackie said, not moving as Maggie moved around the room doing her last-minute business before they left the room for the day. Have to tidy up; you never know when there will be an inspection.

"Well, if you would come to rehearsal," Maggie said, giggling. And then, when she realized Jackie wasn't responding at all, she pulled herself to her full height of nearly six feet and looked Jackie in the eyes.
"Hey, what's going on with you? This witty banter only works if you banter back." Then, her tone and expression changed. "Oh, crap, light dawns on marble head! That's today..."
"Yeah. This afternoon."

"Of course, it's today," Maggie said, rolling her eyes and dropping her terry cloth robe off her shoulders and to the floor where it pooled around her feet. "Why the hell should you be allowed to enjoy the holiday? I mean, seriously... I thought government people got all the holidays off. Why are they even working today?"

Having long ago acclimated herself to the reality of Maggie's immodesty, Jackie turned back to the window, casting her eyes down to the empty sidewalk in front of the house. In roughly 52 minutes, that sidewalk will be flooded with the residents of all four of the houses in this system. It will be a short burst of energy as they blast out of the front of the house and into the vehicles that will take them all to points elsewhere.

"Usually, yeah," Jackie said. "But we both know you don't watch the news, so of course you don't know what's happening." She giggled at that, and heard the closet door behind her slide open as Maggie began to get dressed. "But the girl they are bringing in today. She was on the news. A lot. About a year ago."
When she thought she'd given Maggie enough time to at least put on a layer of clothing, Jackie turned around.
"I'm not supposed to tell you any of this, which is why I didn't tell you before. I mean, it didn't really come up, you know. And, well, you're usually pretty oblivious to what goes on around here."
"Hell, yeah. Rules shmoolz. I say fuck 'em and feed 'em--"
"--fish heads, fish heads, roly poly fish heads," Jackie sang along with Maggie, and they both giggled.

"I mean," Maggie said, "You've either got the assholes running this place with their Gestapo mentality or the jackholes who live in this place and their chicken-coup beta female bullshit. Ugh. I got no time for that. The assholes are easy enough to deal with; just suck it up and don't break their stupid rules."
"Right. Stay out of the spotlight, yes, ma'am, no sir. Go to school, keep the grades up, go to work. Clockwork."
"A Clockwork Orange, more like it," Maggie said.
"Nice," Jackie smiled, looking at the back of Maggie's head. "The point is, though, that this girl, her name is Roberta. Her dad was murdered in front of her. She's a witness."
"Whoa," Maggie said, turning around while pulling a black t-shirt over her head and smoothing it out. "What, is she, like, hiding out here or something? Like witness protection?"
Jackie smirked, closed her eyes, and shook her head, holding her hand to her forehead. Opening her eyes again, looking through her fingers at Maggie, smirked again.

"No, the trial is over and all that. But reporters and lawyers and types like that keep hounding her. So they are basically sneaking her in here today while everyone who went home for Labor Day weekend is coming back."

"Well, now I understand why they picked you," Maggie said. She could tell that Jackie had noticed the shirt she was wearing and also that Jackie was trying very hard not to say anything about it. "You two have a lot in common."

"Yeah. Which is horrible for her. I know, because it was horrible for me. But, at least what I saw was an accident... sort of." Jackie shuddered, her mind trying to go back there... back to that night.
She slammed that door hard. We don't go there.
"So the geniuses in the front offices decided that the two of you would be sisters because of your shared traumatic experiences."
Jackie blinked a couple of times, looking at Maggie.
"What?" Maggie asked.
"Girl, you have been in the system too long."
"Or, maybe just long enough to learn how to poke it without it poking back. I see you looking at this shirt."
"I wasn't going to say anything."
"Yes, you were," Maggie said. "Eventually. You would have." She laughed. "You can't help yourself. But, gold star for trying."
"How the hell did you even get that shirt in here? I know it was Castellano who went through your stuff last time you came back."
"What do I always tell, hmm? Don't what?"
Jackie thought about that, squinted her eyes, and then laughed.
"Don't tell me anything I may be called upon to testify about later."
"Bingo!" Maggie exclaimed, pulling her jeans up and re-straightening the black t-shirt displaying the album cover for Nirvana's _Nevermind_ in all its inappropriate glory.
"There is no way you are getting out of here wearing that shirt," Jackie said.
"Wanna bet?"
"Yeah, you were just now way too confident for me to ever believe I would win that bet."
Maggie laughed, and reached behind her without looking away from Jackie, and pulled a maroon sweatshirt off the top of her dresser in the closet and wiggled it down over her t-shirt.
"Oh, come on," Jackie said. "That is not going to work. They are going to make you raise up that sweatshirt and show them what is under it."
"Darling, if you want to look at my tits, just say so."
"Oh, shut up."

"You see, my dearest Jackson," Maggie said, slipping into her shoes and then twirling around the room, like some aloof character in a golden-age hollywood movie, "They don't catch onto me because I do things like this," and spun toward Jackie, bent down dramtically and kissed Jackie's cheek, said, "toodles, dahling," and twirled toward and out the door, closing it behind her and leaving Jackie standing there alone in the silence.
The bells of St. Thomas chimed, announcing the quarter hour.

That was good, because it didn't give Jackie time to fill the void created by Maggie's departure with those thoughts that piled up against the back of her brain like a brutish horde trying to breach her defenses and pull her down into the prison of her own despair.
7:15 meant she had 10 minutes to spare before she was expected downstairs.
_Ten minutes can be a lifetime if you're living inside my head_, she thought, and decided it would be best if she followed Maggie into the chaos beyond the safety of her bedroom door.
Carpe diem and all that bullshit.

Their conversation would continue exactly where it left off in about one hour from now. That was how it worked around here: the staff tightly controlled the daily schedule to ensure there was as little time as possible for the residents to "get up to no good." Someone was always keeping track of the time.
And someone was always watching.

paragraphs: "You are always watching that kid."

A big, ugly Buick sat in a gravel area in front of the house, with a yard enclosed in a chain-link fence that wouldn't win any awards, but was maintained enough that it wouldn't draw any attention to the house or the person who lived there. There was no shrubbery to speak of, save for some overgrown weeds along the fenceline. The temporarily parked Buick was the most notable thing about the place. That was probably on purpose, as if to say _Nothing to see here, move along._ Neither house on either side had a fence of its own.

Through the binoculars, the driver of the Buick had been seen pulling up and parking in front of the place, to the left of the gate that centered itself on the yard, and parallel to the fence, the driver's side door closest to the fence. The position of the car effectively blocked the view of the driver from the shoulders down until he had passed through the gate and was halfway up the sidewalk, and then one could see a white envelope in the elderly man's left hand. He was elderly, but healthy, walking upright with the confidence of a man with a great deal of experience being in authority, but with the slumped shoulders of a man involved in an activity we loathed.
As he neared the stairs to take him up to the porch, the front door abruptly swung open.

The house was too distant to hear anything from there. The detective sat in a car positioned perfectly from a block over that allowed the entire front of the house to be seen from two blocks away. The road between the road and the one the house sat on was the dividing line between a residential area and the government and commercial heart of downtown. The taller buildings (maxing out in this area at six stories) abruptly ended, giving way to the cookie-cutter houses built during the boom of the 50s.

When the door swung open, the elderly Buick driver stopped momentarily, pulled off his Stetson hat, wiped his brow with the back of his hand, and then slowly moved up the stairs, shaking his head at the man in his mid-twenties standing in the doorway holding the screen door and saying something. As always, the young man looked like he was in a big hurry; he seemed to be trying to rush the old man into the house.

The Detective could tell the man had opened his mouth to say something, decided it wasn't worth the effort, then put his hat back on and walked up the stairs and into the house, past the young man dressed like he had been out partying all night, which he probably had been.
The young man's eyes never left the white envelope.
"I don't know what you're talking about," he said to his partner. "I'm just sitting here enjoying my morning breakfast burrito and my nice lukewarm cup of coffee."

"Well, then, here's to us," Sylvia said, raising her own cup to tap the side of his binoculars. "Just a couple of Rock Spring's finest detectives not doing a thing out of the ordinary on a nationally-celebrated holiday." She giggled, then popped her index finger out and poked the back of his head with one of her long red fingernails.
"Ow! Shit," he said, and pulled the glasses down and looked at her. "What the hell?"
"Yeah, man," she said. "What the hell? I mean, a breakfast burrito and a cold cup of coffee are a pretty shitty cover story if someone were to, say, ask me why we are spying on the sheriff's son."
"We're not spying," Detective Stephenson finally answered after a few seconds of staring at her and blinking. "We're _surveilling_."
He turned back to the window and resumed looking through the binoculars
"Oh, ok," she replied. "'Cause there's a difference."
"Did you see that piece of shit Camaro back there that owner probably still thinks is 'cherry'?"
"You mean the blue one with Missouri plate, 'I-R-O-K-U-6-9'? Couldn't really miss it. Kinda sticks out like a sore thumb."

"See, what's gonna happen here," Stephenson said, continuing to watch through the binoculars as nothing happened, "is that the sheriff there with his big ass Buick Roadmaster is going to leave, and within minutes, that cliché is going to pull up right where the Buick is now. Driver will get out, go inside the house, five minutes later, he's going to leave."
"Wow," Sylvia said. "Really? That obvious?"
"Oh yeah. Kid thinks he has diplomatic immunity... and he's mostly right."
"So," Sylvia said, "I guess a better word would be 'cavalier,' then."

She ducked slightly lower in the seat and turned with her back to the passenger window. Doing so allowed her to see the house her partner was looking at (although without the magnification of his binoculars, she knew, it would be impossible to convince a jury that she could identify anyone). Her new position also allowed her a view of the road the house was on through the rear passenger window, which was the direction from which she assumed the blue sports car would approach the house. This side of that road was all parking lots and businesses, as opposed to the buildings on the opposite side, which were all residences. This afforded them a good view with zero blind spots for the Camaro to disappear into.
Stephenson chuckled.
"Nice job on the location here," she said, shifting her eyes toward Stephenson, then just watching the scene. "It's almost as if you've been scoping this place out for a while."

Traffic was light on this Labor Day, and there wasn't a pedestrian in sight. Even the park a quarter-mile behind them was vacant; apparently the children of Rock Springs took advantage of the holiday and had stayed in bed, which is exactly where Sylvia wished she was right now. Once in a while, she might hear a gate creak or slam, the rattle of a chain-link fence somewhere in the distance, or the call-and-response of distance dogs. Other than that, it seemed even the birds had taken the day off today.
Except, of course, for the jailbirds she and Stephenson were watching.

The shops and boutiques along this street remained closed this morning, but that was nothing unusual because on most days the shops wouldn't be open until 10am, anyway. This was the last block of the downtown area, and all of these shops were locally-owned: a pawn shop/bail bondsman, a hair salon, an accountant, a hobby store Sylvia never saw anyone go into or come out of except the tired and withered old man who owned the place, and a corner diner (Bella Miha, est 1963), which Sylvia never saw completely empty. They were all nicely kept in their Eisenhower-era gray brick-and-mortar, each shop more or less a cubicle within the building, and both the pawn shop and hair salon were highly decorated with vibrant colors, flashing lightsm and displays, and when the girls were in at the salon, you would hear the boppity bop of the latest hip hop from their house stereo echoing off the brick wall partitioning the parking lot across the street from the rest of the neighborhood. Nature has begun to encroach on the entire neighborhood, as this area, once booming, found itself shuttering most of the small industrial shops as the reality of the fragility of the paperless/productless economy came crashing on their heads.

It was another shitty Monday morning in another shitty town in the dying heart of America's once-thriving industrial giant. Nothing was happening. Looking out the fourth-floor window of her shitty apartment, she looked down at the shitty street and all the shitty people walking around just being shitty. Stupid and crazy people wandering up and down the streets, droning in and out of the crumbling stores and businesses along a shitty main street with no trees and no greenery to speak of except for the weeds fighting their way through the plethora of cracks and breaks in the concrete.

The same shitty cracks and breaks she walked on when she would pass those same storefronts on her way to and from her shitty house to her shitty school (though only two of the stores, _Benny's Pizza_ and *Train & Vein*, remained from those thrilling days of yesteryear).

"Everything is shitty, kitty," she said, and slipped her bunny-clad feet off the cafe table in front of the window. They hit the floor with a thump, and she giggled (or was it smirked?; she was so cynical she couldn't tell anymore), then stood and stretched, looking down at the black-and-white 4-year-old who-the-hell-knows-what-breed-this-is cat, who was currently lying in the tiny patch of sun coming in from the bathroom window through the open door.
"Myerrr," she said, looking up, as if to say, _Yes, I believe we have established that._ Her name was Ms. Kitty. Because of course it was. And it was Mizz Kitty, not Miss Kitty, thank you very much.
Moving away from the window, she stepped over the cat (who let out a little noise when the sun was momentarily blocked as the woman passed over) and into the kitchenette area, to refill her coffee.
It was a tiny, shitty apartment. But it was her tiny shitty apartment.
_Shitty town, shitty street,_ she thought.
"Hey, wasn't that a Bill Withers song?" she asked Ms. Kitty, who _Myerr_ed again.
One more cup of coffee and this funk should subside.

Leaning back against the counter sink, she stirred her coffee absently while she looked out the window. She was always looking out the window. From her vantage point, whether here at her window or up in the rooftop garden, she could see the entire downtown area; also, her building was situated to the southeast corner just outside of what was technically the downtown area. South of her was the river, which allowed a good view because the river flattened the terrain. And to the north, the buildings were all lined up perfectly so she could see out across the town, nearly to old ruins in the woods... but not quite. Even with the binoculars she couldn't see that far.

She thought about getting a telescope, but that was a little creepy and potentially civil-rights-violately even for her. Plus, she still wouldn't be able to see through the trees. Or the other barriers which exist only to keep out peeping eyes like hers.

And there it was ... she heard the familiar sound of a truck being taken out of gear every morning, along with the familiar smell of diesel fuel she would forever associate with childhood country fairs. Through the open window, she heard the creaky door open, then close.
Soon, she knew that diesel smell would be replaced by that wonderful smell of freshly-baked bread.
But first, the ball-breaking.

She moved to the window and leaned out, her upper body outside the apartment, and looked down across the street and the big bakery box truck, and the man walking from the door of the truck to the door of the storefront across from her.
"Hey!" she yelled down, and he wasn't even startled. Dammit. "You know, there's this miracle elixir that fixes old creaky doors. It's called WD-40. You should look into that!"

"Good mornin', Lois," he called up, laughing. Herbie could break balls with the best of them. In his left hand, he held out his keys, ready to unlock and move inside. Over his right shoulder, more importantly, he was balancing a tray of something she knew he was going to turn into something tasty and downright sinful. "Shouldn't you be getting ready to cover the parade? Big doin's downtown," he said, making himself laugh harder.
"You know something I don't know?" she asked, also laughing. "We got a renegade band of hardcore prepubescent BMXers wreaking havoc? A baton twirling teen tart attacking terrified townspeople?"
Herbie laughed again. "Hey, you never know. Stranger things have happened in this town."
"Ain't that the damned truth?" she said. "Now get your ass in there and make whatever that is I'm going to regret consuming later."
"Have a good one, _Lois_," he said and turned toward the door as she moved back in through her window.
Then, as an afterthought, she called out, "Happy Labor Day!"
Herbie's arrival was like the personification of Cat Stevens' _Morning Has Broken_.
Her name is not Lois. That was Herbie breaking balls. Lois, as in Lois Lane, from Superman fame.

Most people call her Abby... well, among other things. Abigail Hubbard is her name... and her byline. She's a reporter for _The Rock Springs Chronicle_, the local newspaper with a circulation of about thirty-five thousand... on a good day. And as everyone knows, a good day for circulation is probably a really bad day for someone, if not everyone.

Not always, though. Tonight's edition would be saturated with the events of all the goings-on about town on this warm and wonderful Labor Day. The fairs, the parades, the big fireworks show tonight after the concert in the city park. The features peeps were down there right now unpacking and getting situated.

Abby was not a features peep. She had zero interest in going down there and watching all that stupid pageantry that meant nothing and, ironically, represented a whole lot of labor on what was really supposed to be a national annual sabbath where we all get to not work. Abby also was not a not-work kind of girl, either. What she knew more than anything was that days like these were good for shoving the real news onto page six, and she also knew that big events like this were also a good way to divert attention to things going on elsewhere that might be, shall we say, untoward.

She leaned back against the counter again, stirring her coffee absently, looking out across the window. She could still see over the buildings across the street and down to Main, where crowds were beginning to build. The news trucks were down there, at the staging area to the north in what was once an elementary school playground but was now just an asphalt lot with a decaying building attached to it.

Her view, at least from where she stood, was blocked, but when she was sitting in the windowsill she could see that old school well. And the buildings on this side of Main. Specifically, the police station.

Apparently, Detective Stephenson and his partner thought this was a good day to go snooping around for whatever the powers that be might be up to while the huddled masses were huddling and massing along Main Street. Abby knew this because she had watched his partner's purple Dodge Neon pull into the lot, and before she was halfway across the lot to the building, Stephenson had emerged from the rear door and ushered her toward their not-at-all-conspicuous silver Crown Victoria. Then they had pulled out and off they went, out of the parking lot, taking a left on Franklin, and then disappearing out of her view.
On another day she might've hustled up to the roof to watch where they were going, but today she had her own story to chase that, for once, had nothing to do with Stephenson.

At least, that was what she thought at 8am. By 3pm, she would remember thinking that. She would also wonder why the hell her world so often seemed to revolve around Detective Lloyd "Steve" Stephenson.
She put that out of her mind. Ancient history.

Current events were happening while this town was celebrating, and as if to punctuate that thought, Abby became aware of the sounds of life beginning to pour into the street below her. She moved back to her window and sat back down at her cafe table, this time angling herself so she could watch what was happening in the northwest quadrant of town. That direction, where her view stretched outward, like the shadowy fingers stretching over the landscape, all the way to the forest she couldn't see from here. But what she could see from here was the complex of houses just beyond that old abandoned school where all the news trucks were parked.

New Beginnings, it was called. Local youth group home, run by religious zealots, as is probably the case with most local youth group homes. The four renovated turn-of-the-century houses could hardly be seen themselves, but just enough was visible behind the school and the empty lots that Abby could keep track of the comings and goings. But from 1800 feet away, those comings and goings were generic, and there was no way she was getting closer.

Oh yes, they all knew Abby at New Beginnings. And they didn't seem to particularly care for her. Probably wasn't personal though; most people in charge of children don't like being asked questions about how they are caring for those children, especially religious zealots whose approach to child-rearing is closer to the tactics of the Khmer Rouge than Dr. Spock.

Abby had it on good authority that a new resident was arriving this afternoon. It was being kept quiet because of the nature of the girl's case. The girl was part victim, part culprit, and all of thirteen years old, which meant her identity could not be published. There was a lot of publicity around her case up north, toward the Springfield area. It had made the news and the papers locally, but as things do, it faded quickly in the news churn. The girl was being shipped to Rock Springs because it was far enough away that she might actually be able to have a normal life.
She actually smirked at that loud enough to elicit a dirty look from Ms. Kitty.
"What?" she said to the cat, whose head was lying on the floor, upside down, her white tuft exposed and her yellow eyes appearing to be locked onto Abby's. "You know what goes on there."

Today presented a golden opportunity. The powers that be thought they could hide right out in the open. It was actually a good play. Bring the girl in through the back door, a block away from where every media outlet in the area will be camped, looking in the opposite direction. It was almost brilliant. Maybe.
You know, except for Abby's mole.

Truth be told, and not to be crass, but Abby really didn't care about the story of the little girl being brought in under cover of the light; there were plenty of Springfield/Champaing/Rantoul reporters writing about that story. But following that story might get Abby back to the story that really mattered to her.
The girl from Champaign was moving into the same house as Jackie French. And Jackie French was the real story.

Picking up her binoculars, Abby looked out across the town, and as she was focusing in on the two-story building where the girl in question lived, she saw the familiar smoke plume in her left periphery. And then that heavenly smell of baking bread. She breathed it in deep, held it for a second, then let it out.
_Your moment of zen_, she thought.

But aloud, she said, "Ok, girl, time to get your ass in gear." She dropped her bunny-clad feet to the floor again (this time not coming anywhere near Ms Kitty, who had at some point wandered over to her bowl) and padded off in the direction of her shower, pink terry-cloth robe flying out behind her like a superhero's cape.

paragraphs: If Abby _had_ been able to see as far as those woods, what she would have seen were two bicycles with preteen riders barreling down a well-worn path across farmlands and into those trees like the Devil himself was giving them chase.

They had ignored the No Trespassing signs, slipped through the gaps in the fence without slowing down or getting off their bikes, and breezed into the one area in the entire country that both Abby and Stephenson would agree was the absolute last place a couple of 10-year-old boys should find themselves, no matter how bulletproof and invincible they believed themselves to be.
"We're not even supposed to be out here!" One of the boys yelled, the one bringing up the rear.
"Don't be a pussy, pussy!"

Always came down to that. Every single time. It's like the post-modern rallying cry of the modern adolescent male: _Don't Be A Pussy_. And as he put his foot on the pedal and slowly began to move forward, it occurred to him that, while it might be bullshit to call someone such a thing when they were clearly just thinking in terms of self-preservation, it was also effective.
"You're such an _a-hole_," he said, while pedaling faster to keep up.

They both knew they weren't supposed to be out here. It was simply too far away from home. Which is, of course, why they were out here in the first place. Obviously, if the old guys didn't want them out there, there was something out there they should definitely investigate.

For Jesse, the aforementioned asshole, being this far from home was the only point; the quickest way to get him to do something was to tell him he couldn't do it. Thad's motivations, however, were different and, if he was being honest, probably the reason his parents were so implicit when they voiced that command; they knew his curiosity could get the best of him, so they wanted to keep him safe. But there was irony in their admonitions: The quickest way to get Thad interested in a thing was to paint that thing as mysterious, off limits, and out of bounds.
This is why the boys were up at 5:30. They had meant to get up, get rolling, and be out nearly here by the time the bell from St. Thomas sounded at 7:00.
They were already late.

It hadn't been as easy as Jesse had thought it would be to sneak down the stairs and out the back door, nor had it been as quiet as Jesse assumed it would be to open the side door to the garage (Abby would probably have recommended WD-40). Jesse had also, at one point, said to the neighbor's dog, Lady, that he "knew you were a bitch, but I didn't think you were a snitch," which Thad thought was pretty funny. And the inside of Jesse's family garage looked like an antique store exploded in there like a million years ago.

So that had taken them a good fifteen minutes longer than it should have, and whatever it was that Jesse wanted to do out here (he was keeping it a secret like he was some sort of secret agent), it was also taking longer to get there than he thought. It had taken Thad a while to realize where they were going, and by the time he did, they were pretty much past the point of no return. If they weren't back to be picked up by 9:00, Thad's mother would simply kill him. Jesse's mother would probably kill _him_, too. The parade starts at 10. They were supposed to meet up with the rest of their Scout troop at the "staging area" by 9:30 so everyone could be placed in that row-and-column formation they always took up in parades (Three times a year every year since 2nd grade, ugh).

And as he heard St. Thomas's bell announce the 7:30 mark in the distance, he knew there was no way they were going to make it back. They would be lucky if they got back by the time the parade was over, at this rate.
Jesse clearly had zero spatial intelligence... and might be allergic to actual maps.

Thad pedaled faster, pumping his short legs as hard as he could, but Jesse, who was a good four inches taller than Thad and mostly leg, had pulled far ahead. He was already in the trees, and Thad was still on the path in the field halfway from the road to the trees, probably still in plain view of creepy old man Chalmers, whose property they were currently trespassing on.

Clearly they weren't the first to trespass here, given the well-worn path, but for creepy old man types, seven a.m. was probably their most creepy, hating-little-boys time of the day. And on a holiday like Labor Day, what else did he have to do except sit in his attic with a sniper rifle....
Well, that's what they all told each other, anyway. Crazy Vietnam vet, ready to pick off any little shit who places any of their appendages anywhere on his lawn.

Suddenly feeling like he had a target on his back, Thad pushed himself even harder, praying his foot didn't slip and unleash the shark-toothed metal monster currently taking the form of his pedals that existed only to feast on bare-and-vulnerable shins, as evidenced by the distinct scabbing pattern that already existed on Thad's left shin. _It's_ always _the left one_, he thought. _Maybe mix it up and take a bite out of the right one for a change._

His foot was prone to slipping because this wasn't really his bike. Okay, it was, but it was a hand-me-down, just like nearly everything he owned. It had been repainted and rewelded and had nearly every part replaced over time, but it was still that same bike that came down from Moses or somebody... The name "BRADLEY" might be etched into the top bar (The Nutcracker. Sweet!) because Thad had gotten the bike from Brad, but Brad had gotten it from one of their older cousins. Thad didn't know which one.
But it was probably Chad.

God, his family was weird. Addison, Madison, Bradley, and Thadeus... Addy, Maddy, Brad, and Thad. And whose idea was all that? That's right. Dad. Thad wondered if he could roll his eyes any harder without breaking something.

Up ahead, the Chalmers property ended. The fence cornered to the left; beyond it was the trees. The deep and dark forest that looked right out of every Disney movie he'd ever seen. It was forboding, and Thad thought it might not actually be out of the realm of possibility that Dorothy's apple-throwing trees from _The Wizard of Oz_ might be in there.

"As long as there are no flying monkeys," he said aloud, the word "monkeys," barely above a whisper as he tried to use all his air and energy to push forward, his hair sweaty and his legs beginning to ache; he couldn't remember ever riding a bike this fast for this far or this long.

Once he broke through into that darkness, the temperature seemed to drop ten degrees, and the ground sloped more than ten degrees downward. Holding tightly to the handlebars, he kicked his feet up on the gooseneck of the bike and coasted.
The bike reached a ridiculous level of speed, and Thad giggled like a crazy person as he disappeared into the darkness.
Later, Thad would appreciate that Creepy Old Man Chalmers was, in fact, watching the whole thing through his binoculars from the porch of his massive and ancient white farmhouse.

presentation.excerpt: If Abby had been able to see as far as those woods, what she would have seen were two bicycles with preteen riders barreling down a well-worn path across farmlands and into those trees…

paragraphs: Everyone knew when he said he was going to "walk the perimeter" what he really meant was that he was going to walk around the block and smoke a cigarette. He tried to keep his smoking out of the view of the girls, but they knew, and he knew they knew: they might not see him, but they could smell him. Hell, sometimes he puffed the smoke down so fast that even *he* could smell it. It was a nasty habit, and he wish he could stop, but he had tried several times and in the end it came down to either smoking a cigarette or committing homicide, so he chose to spark up rather than bludgeon some jackass he didn't know the screw with the wrong guy today.

This time, however, he was actually walking the perimeter. He was nevervous. Not in the "Danger, Will Robinson" way, but... there was something afoot. He knew it, but he couldn't prove it. And even if he could prove it, he didn't think it would change anything. When you fight the machinery, you end up like John Henry; even if you win, the fight itself will kill you.

paragraphs: "How you doin' back there, kiddo?"

If this were a movie, this would be the part where Bobbi broke the fourth wall like Ferris Bueller to talk directly to the audience. There was so much in that question that what she really wanted to do was grab the douchebag sitting in the front seat and slam his face into the dash repeatedly until all that was left was a clump of hair and his partner, the driver, staring at her like she was either Quentin Tarantino or Stephen King's villain... Maybe John Carpenter. Yeah, probably John Carpenter because he gets the grossest of all of them, and the dickheads in the front seat both deserved the grossest of grossest deaths.
_How am I doing, indeed..._

This would be the part, in her movie, where she would freeze-frame and then open the car door and step out. If this were a movie. Unfortunately, it is not; it is the real world, and she has to actually stay in the car and deal with it.
In her Tarantino movie, she wouldn't have left, anyway. She would look at the audience and tell them everything that sentence meant to her.

See, Bobbi knew things, because she heard things. Things that she, most of the time, had no interest in hearing. She could hear all the people around here with their petty squabbles, weird quirks, and sometimes sinister agendas. Those things came off people like radiating heat.

Bobbi didn't really hear the little things, because most people didn't really focus on those. Once in a while, she'll catch that weird snippet that she would really love to have explained to her. Like the time she heard that fleeting remark, like "...and get those pants to 9th or her dog might not make it," which is one of the weirdest out-of-context things she ever had flit through her mind, but it was there and then gone, and she had no idea who it had come from.

"Hearing" is not the right word, because that assumes auditory input travelling on sound waves, and that is _not_ what Bobbi means. But in most people's real world, Bobbi's ability doesn't exist and is the stuff of fiction. The type of thing one might actually read in a Stephen King novel or see in a John Carpenter movie... or even Chris Carter, for that matter, because Bobbi is what most people would call a "telepath," although what they mean by that isn't exactly what Bobbi actually experiences. She doesn't "read minds" as much as she receives information from people who are close to her, like a car radio constantly on channel seek mode. Things will come into her brain and then go away. It took her a very long time to realize that the voices she was hearing in her head were actual people and not just her own imaginary friends or demons hanging around...

Things came and went through her brain, just like people come and go in a person's life. Swatches and snippets... _Did I leave the front door unlocked?_ Or _I have to remember to get bread on my way home_ ... the crap that fills people's brains and lives. Most of it, she ignored because it was private and Bobbi didn't know why she had access to it. She felt guilty and a little dirty, like she was spying on the most intimate moments. But it was completely involuntary. God knew there were times when she wished she could just shut it off.
Times like right now. There was nothing she wanted less than to hear the demented shit going on in these two jokers' brains.

_Kiddo_. Bobbi thought this motherucker was lucky she could only read minds and couldn't go the full Carrie on his ass. Calling her "kiddo," as if to confirm her role as the 13-year-old child she was, while at the same time imagining all the things he'd love to do if given the chance.
Bobbi couldn't help that she could pass for a 9-year-old if she tried.

She never tried, but she was shorter than almost all of the girls her age, and when she was in a group of those girls, it probably looked to an outsider like one of the girls was babysitting Bobbi. But two things on her had developed maybe a little ahead of schedule, and Special Agent Questionable Morals up there in the front seat couldn't keep his eyes off of them, believing that if he hid those wandering peepers behind sunglasses with mirror lenses, Bobbi wouldn't know.
You didn't have to be telepathic to get the gist of what that asshole was thinking.
_Wonder what my dad would do if he was here and knew what you were thinking..._

What she got from people wasn't always audio. Sometimes it was visual, and that was so much worse. Sometimes she had to force herself to move away from a person's thoughts, because there are just some heads you don't want to go poking around in. Being in a car, as she currently was, usually gave her some comfort and relief, because it was mostly just her and her dad.
Was. That was the hard word. Was. Had been. Used to.
Never again.

Some of the people she had met over the past year-- most, if she's being honest-- told her repeatedly, redundantly, that her father abused her, that the nature of their dynamic betrayed the contract between a father and daughter. They tossed around words like "inappropriate" (they loved that word) and "exploitative" as if they had any idea what they were talking about. All of their legal and psychosocial bullshit amounted to the same thing: a bunch of highly educated liberal progressives who did see the irony of the way they were shaming her father, although he was really the only victim in the entire situation.
Things didn't go bad because of her father; they went bad because of a psychopath who wanted to do exactly the things they accused her father of doing. When she thought about it
_smell of whiskey... cigar smoke_
and she tried not to
_sound of poker chips... laughter..._
she realized that there was really only one person to blame
_laughter fades... awkward silence_
and that was Bobbi herself
_shouting... sound of glass shattering against the wall..._
because somehow the psychopath knew...
_overturned table, threats, three gunshots..._
and he wanted the goose that laid the golden eggs.
_So much blood, smell of gunsmoke, shouting, pleading, fleeing..._
And then it was darkness. And he was gone. And he wouldn't be back.
Never again.
She didn't cry then. She wasn't going to cry today. Bobbi was getting used to men with their own agendas getting her into cars.

_They_ didn't know what to do with her. Of course, _they_ had no idea what she could do, so they had zero inkling of what her true involvement was. The _they_ that is the Department of Children and Family Services thought she was an exploited victim who should be given every opportunity other children her age were given; the _they_ that is the Illinois justice department were suspicious and knew there was more to the story than what she was telling, and the _they_ who was her family was nonexistent. They didn't give a shit about her when her dad was alive, so why would they give a shit about her now that he is dead? Fuck them.
And that was the way of the world, for her. Her and Daddy against the world, and now Daddy was gone.
One name Daddy never called her was _kiddo_. And never called her kid either, and didn't like it when other people did, either.
"What're you a goat?" he would ask, and she would giggle.

Because they didn't know what to do with her, they were shipping her down to the southern part of the state where she would become someone else's probably. They weren't really interested in her well-being. They were only interested in her testimony in court and her silence when she wasn't in court.

Despite the semi-snappy way they dressed and their appearance of professionalism, the two rejects in the car with her would not make it to the end of the plot of a bad 80s action drama; they would be the no-named guys in the credits: Creepy Agent #1 and Creepy Agent #2, and would exist only to either display the depths of the antagonist's villainy or to show the lengths to which the protagonist's cohort would go to save the protagonist, and they would be remember as well as any henchmen should be remembered... not at all.

_How are you doing?_ If she had a nickel for every time someone had asked her that question in the past year, she would have... well, more money than she has now. It's not always _you_, though. Sometimes, it's _we_, as in, "How are we doing today?"

It's infuriating. Because they don't give a shit how Bobbi is doing. They want her to regurgitate the bullshit they sling at her, like some weird version of semantic tennis, and if she were to actually tell them how she was _really_ doing, they might just shut the fuck up and leave her alone.

She almost chuckled aloud at that thought. Because no, they wouldn't. If she expressed herself for real, they'd hit her with so many pills she'd be like Jack Nicholson at the end of _One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest_, praying Chief would come put a pillow over her face.

Almost chuckled, but didn't. Because they'd ask her what was so funny and she'd either have to tell them the truth about what she found so amusing or lie and say she was thinking about something from earlier, but either way she'd be defending that stupid little betrayal of her body.

As it was, she was realizing right now that she was taking too long to respond to him because she had, actually, lost control of her thoughts, if not her emotions yet. She needed to answer him in some way, and saying, "Well, my dad is dead, I have no home, I have no money, I'm completely dependent on the state, i'm 13 and have at least 4 years before i can get away from you people, so now I'm being shipped down to the deepest depths of the state of Illinois in a city I've never heard of which is 500 miles south of everything I know, to be shoved into a home with a bunch of other people you all think are criminals except that I am even more a criminal because i am being transported in secret by the FBI who can't seem to find anything to charge me with but they really, _really_ want to so they are pretending that the reason they are involved is a concern for my safety, which is probably at least partially true because you all have yet to catch the guy who kidnapped me and killed my dad so how the fuck do you think I am?" was _inappropriate_.

So, instead of saying all that, she looked out the window at all the agricultural scenery passing by. Barbed wire, cornfields, and the smell of either cow or pig shit- she neither knew nor cared which. Up ahead, a highway sign told her that they were 110 miles from Rock Springs, 85 miles from Marion, and 40 miles from Mount Vernon, three places that she had not only never been to, but that she had never heard of.

The fourth place on the list she had heard of... well, sort of. Apparently they were 160 miles from Metropolis, and the number 160 was superimposed over the Superman chest 'S' logo. That was pretty cool. And she definitely needed a hero right now, but she wasn't holding out for one.
No, she said none of that. Just like Jesus in Luke 23:18, she uttered only two words.
"Everything's fine."

Then she looked at herself in the mirrored reflection of Secret Agent Questionable Morals's shades, and stretched out across the back seat, pretending to fall asleep but really just listening to the Go-Go's in her brain because for some reason that particular song kept the creepy voices at bay.
After a few minutes, she was no longer pretending; she was snoring softly and ignoring the others' thoughts completely.
Jeremy was distracted.

As hard as he tried, he couldn't stop looking over at the ugly red house across the street from the parking lot where he was currently trying to herd these Cub Scouts (_Webelos!,_ one of them reminded him. Yeah, that's how well this was going) into position. It should be very simple: rows, columns. 35 _Webelos_ (for those keeping score, that's 35 eleven-year-old boys) who were harder to keep into position than the same number of cats would be; at least with cats, a can opener would get their collective attention. Jeremy couldn't think of a single thing that could unite this pack of eleven-year-olds who were hopped up on whatever sugar-embued sustenance their minivan-drivin' moms had poured down their throats on the way here.

It would have been hard enough trying to get all this together, but the fact that he was less than 100 feet from Jackie right now was making it hard for him to think about anything but walking away from this group of shitheads and march right over there, through the sinking fence and the busted-upsidewalk, over the pothole-ridden street and up to that porch with its black chipped paint and deliver a sililoquey that would make Shakespeare proud and blush at the same time.

There were plenty of other things to distract, too. Like the baton twirlers in their tiny little glittery outfits. Hard to keep your eyes to yourself... Or it would be if he didn't know most of those stuck-up bitches. Right now, they were busying themselves trying to out-pretty each other, but Jeremy saw a couple of them eyeballing him.

He sighed out loud. The mean girls. He could care less about their petty nonsense most days-- it was usually about him and Jackie, or Jackie and this or Jackie and that, so it was white noise-- but today, if given the opportunity, those barracudas would pounce. They would be marching or dancing or whatever the hell they were doing, and if Jeremy didn't keep these Scouts in formation and on time, they were liable to slam into that murder of crows, and then it would be every Webelo for himself.
The very thought of intervening in a war between the mean girls and a pack of eleven-year-old boys sent a shiver down his spine.
"It'll look good on our college applications."
"Yeah, that's what they keep telling me." Jeremy cast a glance back up to Jackie's bedroom window, and then turned to the source of the voice, who had walked up behind him.

"Doesn't mean I have to like getting up this early on a holiday," Devon said, and handed Jeremy a nice warm cup of coffee. Luke warm, actually. Seeing his reaction after Jeremy took an embittered sip, Devon added, "I got up fifteen minutes late. Just in time to hit that beautiful solid wall of unmoving traffic."
Jeremy laughed.
"Dude, you're early for you."
Devon elbowed him in the wrist, and Jeremy almost spit out the god-awful gas station coffee. He only held it in out of respect for the grass. It did nothing to deserve that shitty coffee.
"Hey, fuck you, _marricone_!" Devon said.

Devon was not Hispanic in any way. Jeremy was pretty sure that his Spanish-speaking skill didn't extend far beyond Americanized versions of Spanish curse words. Devon was a 5-foot-11-inch tall black man who spent most of his time at the gym trying to get what he called "that Michael Jordan v-cut." It was working.

As much as it sucked for Devon, the truth was his best bet to get the fuck out of this town was a sports scholarship. That said nothing about Devon and everything about this backward-ass town and what they considered tolerable levels of pigmentation.
No, _marricone_ was just Devon's new favorite word. Most of the guys said motherfucker; Devon said _marricone_. For now. Until he was over _Scarface_ and moved on to the next thing.
"I see you looking up at her window, Mr. Stalker," Devon said. "You know she's not up there, right? They got a pretty tight schedule there; they aren't in their rooms much unless they're in trouble."
"Yeah, I know," Jeremy said. "I just keep hoping that she sneaks up to look out here."

Devon turned and waved to the massive, still gathering crowd. On the one side, streaming down the street, all of the floats and bands and soon this pack of little shits, in the middle all of these press trucks as though this were the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, lining Main Street were all the people begin to get in position to watch, there were dozens of parents and many dozens of parade participants ranging from the day care center to the National Guard-- who, by the way, had brought a tank with them-- to the Lion's Club.
"What the fuck makes you think she could see you if she _did_ look out here? It's a goddam circus out here."
"No," Jeremy said, "the circus is tonight. That's what those big tents are for out at the park."
"Again," Devon said, "fuck you, mariccone."
"Do you know what that word actually means?" Jeremy asked, laughing. "Because you talking about my girlfriend and then calling me that kinda makes me think you don't."
"Maybe Jackie is your beard."
Jeremy just looked at him and blinked. Devon looked back and also blinked.
Then Jeremy burst out laughing.
"Oh, fuck _you_, marricone!"
Devon looked around again, but this time focusing.
"Ok, man, you got the chart? We should get this show on the road."
Jeremy pulled off his backpack and unzipped it. He pulled out a blue folder with the gold BSA log on it.
"Right here," he said. "Just waitin' for your slow ass to show." He stood up and opened the folder. "Pretty sure not everyone is here yet."

The boys in their uniforms, some military inspection ready, some barely past the word "disheveled," were clumped up, as boys do. Laughing, shoving, and generally looking suspicious. But the clumping made it easy to count them.
"I got twenty-eight," Jeremy said.
"Twenty-nine," Devon said. "That kid over there who thinks no one can see him."
Jeremy looked over and just past all the other kids was one boy, leaning against the school building in the deep shadow created by the concrete stairs leading up to the side entrance.
"Yep," Jeremy said. "Got 'im."
"Two more coming in from the side of the parking lot, your 11 o'clock."
"Nice. You're like a sniper."
Devon snickered. "A real sniper would be up there in Jackie's window. That would be the perfect crow's nest right now."
"You _just_ said that she wouldn't even be able to make me out in this crowd."
"I was giving you shit."
"Mm-hmm. So, we're missing five."

"Probably the single dad crowd," Devon said and laughed. "Why you think I'm always late? I get it from my pops. No matter how hard he tries, he can never get all that shit done in the morning that ma used to do. And he really does try. He _comically_ tries."
Devon was a champ. To look at him, you would never know how devastated he had been the two years after his mother lost her battle with cancer.

"Sometimes I swear I hear her giggle at him or do that _tsk-tsk-tsk_ thing she always did when he was _almost_ right... but not quite." Devon giggled himself, closed his eyes, took in a breath, and rubbed his eyebrows. "You know, like that time he got us all to school exactly on time on a particularly gold-ribbon morning, and then two hours later he had to pick up my little sister from school because lactose-intolerant children should not be using actual milk on their cereal."
"Oh my God, dude," Jeremy said. "I think you were just channeling her. You even _tsk_-ed."
Jeremy could tell that made Devon happy.
And that lasted about two seconds, because when he opened his eyes, they immediately widened and he slapped the back of those giant hands into Jeremy's chest.
"Speaking of moms," he said. "We've got a mad mom making a beeline right toward us." Then after a pause, he said, "And by us, I think I mean you... You might need protection."
Jeremy turned to see what Devon was talking about, bracing himself, then instantly relaxed.
"No, it's cool," he said. "I know her."

Before he could expand on that, the woman was on them, moving faster than visible gait would have said she could; she was waving her arms and becoming more and more hysterical with every passing second.

And this wasn't really like her. She was in her early thirties, and usually she was the mom all the other moms were jealous of in a lot of ways. Right now, she looked straight out of her mind. Her hair wasn't done; she was still in her pajamas with a robe thrown over them, and Jeremy knew she would _never_ leave the house like that... Unless--
"Jeremy!" She yelled, running up to him but not invading his space. Being this close to someone she knew seemed to help her get a little bit of a grip.
He stepped forward and bent down a little. She was very short.
"Mrs. Zikas? What's wrong?"
She took a deep breath, and through what was clearly fear and worry, she said, "Please tell me Thad and Jesse are here! I can't find them anywhere!"
